Definitions, composition, osmolarity, tonicity, indications and precautions.

6 IV fluid references Tap a fluid to expand

Definition

A sterile 0.9% sodium chloride solution for IV infusion. The supplied reference identifies it as an isotonic electrolyte replenisher.

Composition

Each 100 mL contains sodium chloride 900 mg. Per liter: sodium 154 mmol and chloride 154 mmol.

Osmolarity
308 mOsm/L
Tonicity
Isotonic
pH
4.5–7.0

Clinical Uses / Indications in Supplied Reference

  • Replacement of fluid and electrolytes
  • The supplied image lists blood transfusion, diabetic ketoacidosis, metabolic alkalosis, hypercalcemia and hyponatremia.

Nursing Considerations & Precautions

  • Assess volume status, serum sodium/chloride and renal/cardiac status.
  • Monitor intake and output, vital signs and signs of fluid overload.
  • For blood transfusion, follow facility policy and use only the compatible fluid and blood-administration setup specified by the blood bank.

Definition

A balanced isotonic crystalloid solution containing multiple electrolytes, including sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride and lactate.

Composition

Per 1,000 mL (as shown): sodium 130 mmol, potassium 4 mmol, calcium 1.4 mmol, chloride 109 mmol and lactate 28 mmol. The label also lists sodium chloride, sodium lactate, potassium chloride and calcium chloride.

Osmolarity
Not stated in supplied image
Tonicity
Isotonic
pH
6.0–7.5

Clinical Uses / Indications in Supplied Reference

  • Mild or severe dehydration
  • Burns
  • Hypovolemia resulting from third-space fluid shifts
  • Fluid loss in the lower gastrointestinal tract
  • Acute blood loss
  • Replacement of fluid and pH buffers

Nursing Considerations & Precautions

  • Monitor hemodynamic status, fluid balance and electrolytes.
  • Use caution in patients with impaired renal function or conditions affecting potassium, calcium or fluid handling.
  • Consider calcium content and medication/line compatibility; follow institutional guidance.

  • The supplied image lists hypovolemic shock, hemorrhagic shock and certain cases of acidosis.

Nursing Considerations & Precautions

CLINICAL REFERENCE

IV Cannula Reference

Peripheral intravenous (PIV) cannulation • Gauge sizes • Color coding • Typical flow rates • Nursing care

7 gauge sizes Color identification Nursing quick guide

What is an IV cannula?

A peripheral intravenous (PIV) cannula is a short, flexible catheter inserted into a peripheral vein to provide venous access for prescribed fluids, medications, and compatible blood components. After successful placement, the introducer needle is withdrawn and the flexible catheter remains in the vein.

Key points

  • Gauge number and catheter diameter are inversely related: a lower gauge number generally indicates a larger catheter diameter.
  • Choose the smallest gauge and shortest catheter that can safely deliver the prescribed therapy at the required rate.
  • Color coding is commonly standardized, but always verify the actual manufacturer's packaging and instructions for use.

Nursing Responsibilities

Before insertion
  • Verify the clinical indication and prescribed therapy.
  • Assess vein condition, site suitability and patient factors.
  • Explain the procedure and check relevant allergies, including antiseptic or dressing products.
  • Perform hand hygiene and prepare equipment.
During insertion
  • Use aseptic technique and appropriate skin antisepsis.
  • Allow antiseptic to dry according to product instructions.
  • Avoid touching the prepared site unless aseptic technique is maintained.
  • Follow institutional policy and device instructions.
After insertion
  • Secure with an appropriate sterile dressing.
  • Keep the site clean, dry and visible when possible.
  • Label and document insertion details according to facility policy.
  • Assess patency before use according to protocol; never force-flush.
Ongoing monitoring
  • Inspect and assess the site regularly.
  • Check for pain, redness, warmth, swelling, leakage or resistance.
  • Review ongoing need and remove when no longer indicated.
  • Document assessment, interventions and patient response.

Phlebitis

Inflammation of the vein. Watch for pain, tenderness, warmth, redness or a palpable venous cord.

Infiltration

Non-vesicant fluid enters surrounding tissue. Possible signs include swelling, coolness, discomfort and slowed infusion.

Extravasation

Vesicant medication leaks into tissue and may cause injury. Stop the infusion and follow the drug-specific extravasation protocol immediately.

Occlusion / Dislodgement

May present as absent flow, resistance, leakage or catheter movement. Do not force-flush a resistant catheter.

Local or bloodstream infection

Assess for increasing redness, warmth, drainage, tenderness or systemic signs. Escalate concerns according to facility protocol.

Clinical Safety Reminder

This is an educational quick reference, not a substitute for competency-based training, clinical judgment, manufacturer instructions for use or institutional policy. IV cannulation should be performed only by trained and authorized personnel. Gauge colors and flow rates can vary by manufacturer; verify the actual product label.

Sinus Rhythms & Rate Variants

Adult reference patterns. Rate and clinical significance depend on the patient.

Normal Sinus Rhythm

Normal
60–100 bpm
Rate60–100 bpm
RhythmRegular
Key ECG Features

Upright P before every QRS; PR 0.12–0.20 s; QRS <0.12 s.

Organized sinus rhythm with consistent P-QRS relationship and normal adult rate.

Clinical note: A normal reference pattern; interpret in context of symptoms, age and the full 12-lead ECG.

Sinus Bradycardia

Normal / slow
<60 bpm
Rate<60 bpm
RhythmRegular
Key ECG Features

Sinus P before each QRS; PR usually 0.12–0.20 s; QRS usually narrow.

Sinus rhythm at a rate below 60 bpm. May be normal in some trained or sleeping individuals.

Clinical note: Assess perfusion, symptoms, medications and underlying cause; a low rate alone does not determine treatment.

Sinus Tachycardia

Normal / fast
>100 bpm
Rate>100 bpm
RhythmRegular
Key ECG Features

Sinus P before each QRS; usually narrow QRS; rate commonly 100–150 bpm in adults.

Sinus rhythm faster than 100 bpm, often a response to fever, pain, anxiety, dehydration or other physiologic stress.

Clinical note: Look for and address the underlying cause; assess hemodynamic status.

Abnormal Rhythms & Acute Coronary Syndrome Patterns

Includes rhythm strips and illustrative ischemia patterns. These are teaching examples, not diagnostic 12-lead ECGs.

Atrial Fibrillation (AF)

Abnormal
Variable
RateVariable
RhythmIrregularly irregular
Key ECG Features

No consistent discrete P waves; fibrillatory baseline; irregular R-R intervals; QRS often narrow.

Disorganized atrial electrical activity with an irregular ventricular response.

Clinical note: Assess stability and stroke risk; requires clinical evaluation and rhythm confirmation.

Atrial Flutter

Abnormal
Atrial ~250–350 bpm
RateAtrial ~250–350 bpm
RhythmOften regular; ventricular response varies
Key ECG Features

Sawtooth flutter waves; atrial activity may conduct in fixed or variable ratios; QRS often narrow.

Organized rapid atrial rhythm with flutter waves, often with 2:1, 3:1 or variable AV conduction.

Clinical note: Assess ventricular rate and stability; do not assume a fixed conduction ratio from a short strip.

Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)

Abnormal
Often 150–250 bpm
RateOften 150–250 bpm
RhythmUsually regular
Key ECG Features

Typically narrow-complex, regular tachycardia; P waves may be hidden or occur just after QRS.

A rapid rhythm arising above the ventricles; exact mechanism needs clinical interpretation.

Clinical note: Assess pulse and hemodynamic stability; urgent escalation for hypotension, chest pain, altered mental status or shock.

Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)

Abnormal / urgent
Often 100–250 bpm
RateOften 100–250 bpm
RhythmOften regular
Key ECG Features

Wide QRS complexes, usually ≥0.12 s; P waves may be absent or dissociated.

Rapid rhythm originating in the ventricles; may be pulsed or pulseless and can deteriorate.

Clinical note: Potential emergency. Check responsiveness and pulse, activate emergency response and follow ACLS/local protocol.

Ventricular Fibrillation (VF)

Abnormal / emergency
Not measurable
RateNot measurable
RhythmChaotic
Key ECG Features

Disorganized waveform with no identifiable P waves or organized QRS complexes.

Chaotic ventricular electrical activity with no effective cardiac output.

Clinical note: Cardiac arrest rhythm: activate emergency response, begin CPR and use AED/defibrillator per protocol.

Asystole

Abnormal / emergency
None
RateNone
RhythmNo organized rhythm
Key ECG Features

Near-flat baseline without discernible ventricular activity; verify leads, gain and connections; exclude fine VF.

Absence of detectable ventricular electrical activity on the monitor/ECG.

Clinical note: Cardiac arrest rhythm: activate emergency response and follow CPR/ACLS protocol; not a shockable rhythm.

ST-Elevation Pattern (STEMI concern)

Abnormal / urgent
Varies
RateVaries
RhythmVaries
Key ECG Features

ST-segment elevation in anatomically contiguous leads may indicate acute myocardial injury; changes depend on lead and context.

A schematic example of ST elevation; STEMI diagnosis requires a full 12-lead ECG and clinical criteria.

Clinical note: Treat as time-critical when suspected: urgent clinical assessment and escalation; do not diagnose from this single illustrative strip.

NSTEMI – Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction

Abnormal / urgent – ACS
Rate varies
ECG patternMay show ST depression / T inversion
BiomarkerCardiac troponin elevated
Key ECG & Diagnostic Features

May show new/dynamic horizontal or down-sloping ST depression and/or T-wave inversion in contiguous leads. ECG can also be nonspecific or appear normal; ECG alone cannot diagnose or exclude NSTEMI.

NSTEMI is an acute myocardial infarction without persistent diagnostic ST-segment elevation. Diagnosis is based on the clinical presentation, ECG assessment and a rise/fall in cardiac troponin with at least one value above the assay's 99th-percentile upper reference limit, interpreted in context.

Clinical note: Obtain prompt clinical assessment and serial ECG/troponin testing as indicated by protocol. A normal or nondiagnostic ECG does not rule out ACS. ST depression in V1–V3 may suggest posterior MI and warrants appropriate posterior-lead assessment when clinically indicated.

Basic ECG Components

P Wave

Atrial depolarization.

PR Interval

Beginning of P wave to beginning of QRS; usual adult range 0.12–0.20 seconds.

QRS Complex

Ventricular depolarization; commonly 0.06–0.11 seconds in adults.

ST Segment

Early phase after ventricular depolarization; assess elevation or depression in the appropriate leads.

T Wave

Ventricular repolarization.

R–R Interval

Time between consecutive R waves; helps assess rate and rhythm regularity.

Systematic 6-Step ECG Reading

  1. Check patient & tracing: confirm patient details, calibration, paper speed, and lead placement.
  2. Calculate rate: regular rhythm: 300 ÷ large squares between R waves; irregular rhythm: count QRS complexes in 10 seconds × 6.
  3. Assess rhythm: regular or irregular; identify whether P waves are present and related to QRS complexes.
  4. Measure intervals: PR, QRS and QT/QTc; compare with age- and context-appropriate references.
  5. Review axis and morphology: P waves, QRS shape, R-wave progression and signs of chamber enlargement or conduction block.
  6. Assess ST segments and T waves: look for ischemic or other repolarization changes; interpret all 12 leads together.

Clinical Safety Reminder

These are simplified teaching strips, not real patient ECGs. A single-lead rhythm strip cannot establish every diagnosis, and a STEMI assessment requires a complete 12-lead ECG plus clinical context. If a patient is unstable or cardiac arrest is suspected, prioritize immediate assessment, emergency activation and current facility/ACLS protocols.
